summary: Flaky: storefront call-budget tests fail under load, and one fails OPEN (TKT-216 gate incidental)
description:
**Flaky under load, found while gating TKT-216.**

`web/storefront/test/page-call-budget.test.ts` (TKT-208's call-budget proof) fails three of its six
cases when the machine is busy:

```
× event list renders on exactly one upstream call      (timeout at 5000ms)
× event detail renders on exactly one upstream call    (timeout at 5000ms)
× festival detail renders on exactly one upstream call (expected length 1, got 2)
```

**It is not a regression.** Verified by checking out the parent commit (`a05d5cc6`, a docs-only
change sitting on a gate that was green) and reproducing all three failures there. Verified further
by re-running with `--testTimeout=30000`: **6 passed, twice.** The transform step alone takes ~9.7s
in these runs, against a 5s per-test default.

**Why it matters beyond the noise.** The third failure is the interesting one: it does not time out,
it counts **two** upstream calls where the budget allows one. That is the assertion TKT-208 exists to
make, and if load can make it report two calls, then the test cannot distinguish "the page made a
second call" from "the machine was busy". A call-budget proof that fails open under load is not
proving the budget.

**Suggested direction (not a decision):**
- Raise the per-test timeout for this file so a slow transform cannot be read as a budget violation.
- Separately, work out whether the 2-call observation is a genuine second fetch triggered by a
  timeout/retry path, or an artefact of the stub counting a cancelled request. Those need different
  fixes, and only the second is harmless.

Do not simply raise the timeout and close it: that hides the second question.

---

**Update (TKT-216 gate, same session).** The per-test timeout in that file was raised to 30s, because
the gate must be green and the 5s default was turning machine load into a reported budget violation.
The three failures stop reproducing.

**That change closes the noise, not this ticket.** The substantive question is untouched and is the
reason this ticket stays open:

> one of the three observed failures did NOT time out — it counted **two** upstream calls where the
> budget allows one.

So the assertion can still fail **open**. What remains to determine is whether a second fetch is ever
genuine (a retry path, a cancelled request the stub double-counts) or purely an artefact. Those need
different fixes and only one of them is harmless. A comment in the test now says the same thing, so
whoever raises the timeout again does not read it as resolved.

governingAdrs.why: Rule 3 (frontends are call-frugal: one call per page view, not per widget) is the invariant this test proves. VERIFY exact filename at brief time.
governingAdrs.constrains: The budget itself is not re-litigated by this ticket — only the test's ability to measure it honestly.

governingAdrs.why: The SSR cache owns the minutes tier, and client islands hydrate browser-side where this test does not observe them. The test's own header comment (:13-16) records that a green result does NOT mean the page makes one request in production.
governingAdrs.constrains: A fix must not extend the assertion to client-island reads — that is TKT-177's, explicitly.

governingTests.invariant: An in-test comment left by TKT-216 warning that raising the timeout does NOT close this ticket, and naming the fail-open question. It is a live tripwire against the obvious wrong fix; it must be UPDATED (not deleted) when the fail-open path is actually closed, or it will keep warning about a question that has been answered.

Records that the first version of this test called the api.ts wrappers directly and proved nothing about the page — an ai-review finding, explicitly warned against in the ticket's own plan-review. Any refactor that injects a clock must keep rendering the REAL page module through Astro's container.

The render must return 200 AND every repeated child must appear in the HTML. Added in ai-review because a count alone is a weak oracle — a page that short-circuits to 503 spends exactly one call too. A fix must not weaken these.

Already accepts `fetchImpl` and `now` for injection — the seam this fix needs exists. The class also documents a KNOWN unclosed gap: after a backward wall-clock step an entry can outlive its TTL in real time, and closing that needs a monotonic clock source, which would change the injected-clock contract shared with the middleware and the cache's own tests. This ticket must not silently take that on.

context.notes: EXCLUDED from the TKT-231/242 grouping deliberately (owner decision, 2026-08-24). Those two are Go/PostgreSQL smoke tests failing in one shared database at the same helper; this is a Vitest storefront test with no database. Different runtime, different mechanism — bundling would have put a false shared-cause claim in a closeout. What the three DO share is only the symptom class (load-sensitive), which is not a cause.

<!-- sdlc:stage=backlog kind=readiness -->
### Implementation readiness — CONCERNS (shaped 2026-08-08)

Filed with a good description and never shaped, so Gate 1 has been hard-blocking it. Shaped now.

| Criterion | Status | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Objective | OK | The assertion must fail closed, not open |
| Scope | OK | The budget test and the fetch path behind it |
| Uncertainties | **WARN** | Genuine second fetch vs stub artefact — unanswered, and it IS the ticket |
| Dependencies | OK | None; the TKT-216 timeout bump already isolated the signal |
| Approach | **WARN** | Follows from the uncertainty; cannot be settled in shaping |
| AC verifiable | OK | Must demonstrate the test can still fail |
| Context-mémo | OK | Re-resolved today |

**Concern worth stating plainly:** two `open` items would normally block Gate 1, and they are left
open deliberately — this is an *investigation* ticket whose product is an answer, not a diff. If the
owner prefers, it should be re-typed as a **Spike** with the fix as a follow-up; that is a cleaner
fit for the pipeline than a Story carrying two open uncertainties.

**The reason to prioritize it anyway:** this is the only known assertion in the repo that can pass
while the property it proves is false. Per `AGENTS.md`, a fixture that cannot show the negative is a
recurring defect class here (TKT-61, and the "fixture too small" learning). This is that class,
caught in the act.

<!-- sdlc:stage=backlog kind=summary -->
### Fresh reproduction of BOTH halves, from TKT-140's gate run (2026-08-09)

Not a new ticket - adding evidence here rather than filing a duplicate, because this ticket already
names the exact shape and `web/storefront/test/page-call-budget.test.ts:129-134` already records that
it is **not closed**.

Observed while running `make check` for TKT-140 (a Go smoke-test-only change that cannot affect this
suite - `test-ts` is `pnpm -r test` and touches no Go). One gate run produced **both** documented
failure modes in the same file, in one invocation:

```
FAIL  test/page-call-budget.test.ts > ... > event list renders on exactly one upstream call
  Error: Test timed out in 30000ms.

FAIL  test/page-call-budget.test.ts > ... > event detail renders on exactly one upstream call
  AssertionError: expected [ ...(2) ] to have a length of 1 but got 2
    at test/page-call-budget.test.ts:122:37
```

**The second one is the half this ticket says is still open** - it did not time out, it counted TWO
upstream calls where the budget allows one. The in-file comment predicted exactly this ("That
assertion can therefore still fail OPEN, and whether a second fetch is ever genuine - a retry path,
or a cancelled request the stub counts twice - is an open question").

#### The condition that produced it, measured

The machine was at **load average ~30 on 16 cores** (~2x oversubscribed), caused by 24 orphaned
`codex-companion` shells from an unrelated session burning ~64% CPU each for 13 hours. That is the
strongest hint yet about the open half's mechanism: **the double count appeared only under heavy
CPU oversubscription**, never when unloaded.

Controlled runs on the same file, same commit, same machine:

| Run | Tree | Load | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| inside `make check` | TKT-140 change present | ~30 | 2 failed (1 timeout, 1 double-count) |
| standalone | change **stashed**, tree == `origin/main` | idle | 6 passed |
| standalone | change present | idle | 6 passed |
| inside `make check`, after killing the orphans | change present | ~5 | **179/179 passed** |

So: reproducible under load, not reproducible idle, and independent of the tree under test.

#### What this suggests for whoever picks this up

The timeout half is understood (Astro's vite transform is slow on a busy machine; TKT-218's 30s
already mitigates it). For the **open** half, the load-correlation points at the stub's counting
rather than at a genuine second fetch: under CPU starvation a request that is cancelled or retried
at the transport layer could plausibly be observed twice by `stubFetch` while the page still renders
one logical read. Worth testing that hypothesis directly - assert on distinct URLs plus a
render-once marker, rather than on raw call count - before concluding the storefront has a real
double-read.

Recording the load figure specifically because "flaky under load" was previously qualitative; there
is now a number and a reproduction recipe.

<!-- sdlc:stage=backlog kind=readiness -->
**Re-shaped 2026-08-24. Verdict: READY — 8/8 `met`.** The two items that were `open` are both closed, one by execution and one by an owner decision.

### `uncertainties` — answered by running it, not by reasoning

The ticket's central question was whether the 2-call observation is a genuine second fetch or an artefact of the stub counting a cancelled request. **It is genuine.**

`PageDataCache` measures freshness against a **wall clock**. `ageOf()` is `upstreamAgeSeconds + elapsed`, the stub serves `max-age=300` with no `Age` header, so an entry stays fresh for 300 seconds of *wall* time. A starved SSR process that loses more than `max-age` between two reads of one URL misses and re-fetches.

Reproduced directly, with the cache's own injected-clock seam:

```
calls for two gets, normal clock: 1
calls after a 301s stall:         2
```

So the stub counts correctly and the page really does fetch twice. The harmless reading is ruled out — which matters, because it was the reading that would have justified closing this with a widened assertion.

### `approach` — Gate 1 decision, now sharpened by the diagnosis

The direction you chose was *"make the assertion fail closed either way"*. With the mechanism known it becomes concrete: give the cache a **deterministic clock** for this test — the constructor already takes `now`, so the seam exists — and let the fixture decide elapsed time instead of machine load. Same treatment TKT-233 and TKT-232 applied: assert the dependency edge, not a wall clock.

Two fixes explicitly rejected, both of which look right:

- **Raise the timeout again.** The test's own comment at `:124-133` warns against exactly this. It addresses the three *timeout* failures and is silent on the fail-open one.
- **Widen the assertion to `<= 2`.** That *is* the fail-open defect.

### One trap carried into the mémo

`cache.ts` documents a gap it deliberately did not close: after a *backward* wall-clock step, an entry can outlive its TTL in real time, and fixing it needs a monotonic clock source — which would change the injected-clock contract the cache shares with the middleware and its own tests. This ticket must not quietly take that on. It is a different ticket.

### Why this is not grouped with TKT-231/242

Those two are Go smoke tests failing at one helper in one shared PostgreSQL database. This is a Vitest test with no database. They share a *symptom class* — load-sensitive — which is not a cause. Grouping them would have put a shared-mechanism claim in a closeout that the code contradicts.

objective.note: The call-budget assertion cannot report a violation that machine load caused, and cannot pass while a genuine second fetch happens. It must fail CLOSED.

scope.note: web/storefront/test/page-call-budget.test.ts and whatever in the storefront fetch path explains a second call. Not a re-litigation of TKT-208's budget itself.

uncertainties.note: ANSWERED at shaping, by execution rather than inference. The 2-call observation is a GENUINE second fetch, not a stub artefact. Mechanism: PageDataCache measures freshness against a WALL clock (Date.now, cache.ts). ageOf() = upstreamAgeSeconds + elapsed; the stub serves max-age=300 with no Age header, so an entry is fresh for 300s of WALL time. A starved SSR process that loses more than max-age of wall time between two reads of the same URL misses and re-fetches. Reproduced directly: constructing PageDataCache with an injected clock and stepping it 301s between two get() calls on one URL yields calls=2 (fresh clock yields 1). So the stub counts correctly and the page really does fetch twice.

dependencies.note: None. The 30s timeout raised during TKT-216's gate already removed the load-induced noise, so the remaining signal can be studied in isolation.

approach.note: Owner decision at Gate 1 (2026-08-24): make the assertion fail CLOSED regardless of which diagnosis won — and the diagnosis is now known, which sharpens it. The budget assertion must not be able to read wall-clock starvation as a budget violation, while still failing if the page genuinely adds a second read. Direction: give the cache a deterministic clock for this test (the constructor already accepts `now`), so elapsed time is decided by the fixture rather than by machine load. That is the same treatment TKT-233/TKT-232 applied — assert the dependency edge, not a wall clock. Explicitly REJECTED: raising the timeout again (the test's own comment at :124-133 warns against exactly that, and it addresses the timeout failures, not the fail-open one); and widening the assertion to `<=2` (that is the fail-open defect being fixed). NOTE the injected clock must NOT be threaded so far that the test stops rendering real .astro modules through the container — the file's own comment at :76-84 records that calling the api.ts wrappers directly was a defect found in ai-review.

first_slice.note: Reproduce the 2-call observation deliberately (load the machine, or drive the stub directly) so the question can be answered from evidence rather than inference.

success.note: A test that fails when a second upstream call genuinely happens, and passes under load. Prove the failing direction works - a budget proof that cannot fail is the defect being fixed.
